author: sada1708
title: How Bad Data Tricks Good Models: Sampling & Sampling Bias
body:
You build a model with a high validation accuracy. You deploy it. Two weeks later it's making wildly wrong predictions, and your team lead wants to know why.

Here's the uncomfortable truth: when a model fails catastrophically in production, the culprit is rarely a bug in the code, too few transformer layers, or a bad hyperparameter sweep. Nine times out of ten, the real problem was decided before you ever opened a notebook — in how the data was sampled.— it's bad sampling.

Data science runs on one unforgiving law: garbage in, garbage out. If your sample doesn't mirror the real world, your model isn't learning the truth. It's learning a very convincing lie. Here's everything you need to know about sampling methods, how bias sneaks into your pipelines anyway, and how to stop it from quietly sabotaging your production models.

**Part 1: Sampling Methods**

Sampling splits into two camps: probability sampling (random, generalizable) and non-probability sampling (convenient, risky).

![fig1 sampling tree](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Laxminarayen/InceptezGenAI-Batch26/main/data/uploads/articles/mrx6kgfhhgu43j-fig1-sampling-tree.jpg)

**Probability sampling — every unit has a known chance of selection:**

•	**Simple Random Sampling**: every data point has an identical probability of selection. df.sample(n=1000) — works when your population is homogeneous.
•	**Stratified Sampling**: split into subgroups, sample proportionally within each. Critical for imbalanced problems like fraud detection — train_test_split(X, y, stratify=y) preserves class ratios.
•	**Systematic Sampling**: every k-th record after a random start — e.g., sampling every 100th API log. Risky if your data has a periodic cycle.
•	**Cluster Sampling**: randomly pick whole clusters (stores, zip codes) and sample within them — 50 stores out of 10,000 instead of a few customers everywhere.

**Non-probability sampling — faster, cheaper, harder to generalize:**

•	**Convenience**: scraping one forum because it's easy. Your model learns that forum's voice, not the general public's.
•	**Purposive**/Judgmental: hand-picking "typical" cases — efficient, but exposed to whoever's picking.
•	**Quota**: fills subgroup targets non-randomly.
•	**Snowball**: participants recruit participants — great for hard-to-reach populations, but produces correlated clusters.

**Part 2: What Is Sampling Bias?**

Sampling bias happens when certain members of your population are systematically more or less likely to end up in your sample. Your dataset stops mirroring reality and becomes a distorted version of it.

![fig2 biased sample](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Laxminarayen/InceptezGenAI-Batch26/main/data/uploads/articles/mrx6p060jzvbrz-fig2-biased-sample.jpg)

Feed that into a pipeline and the model learns the distortion as fact — confidently, and without throwing a single error.

**Part 3: The Biases That Sabotage ML**

**1. Undercoverage Bias.** Entire segments never make it into your sampling frame.

The 1936 Literary Digest poll surveyed 10 million Americans via telephone books and car registries, predicting a landslide for Alf Landon. FDR won in a historic landslide instead — the sampling frame quietly excluded lower-income voters before a single question was asked.

![fig6 literary digest](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Laxminarayen/InceptezGenAI-Batch26/main/data/uploads/articles/mrx6rck4601xqm-fig6-literary-digest.jpg)

**_ML impact:_** a credit model trained only on urban online applicants fails the moment it meets rural or walk-in applicants.

**2. Survivorship Bias. **Your dataset only contains what passed through a filter — the failures vanish.

Abraham Wald's WWII bomber problem: the military examined returning planes, saw damage clustered in the wings, and almost reinforced the wings. Wald pointed out that planes hit in the engine never made it back to be studied — the armor belonged where returning planes had no holes.

![fig3 survivorship](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Laxminarayen/InceptezGenAI-Batch26/main/data/uploads/articles/mrx6sg01d12p9g-fig3-survivorship.jpg)

**_ML impact:_** a "what predicts startup success" model trained only on companies that still exist has silently deleted every failure — the group you most needed to learn from.

**3. Self-Selection Bias.** Participants opt themselves in, usually because they feel strongly.

Amazon and Yelp reviews mostly come from the thrilled or the furious — the satisfied middle stays silent.

![fig7 self selection](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Laxminarayen/InceptezGenAI-Batch26/main/data/uploads/articles/mrx6tk2ljk92u1-fig7-self-selection.jpg)

**_ML impact: _**a sentiment model trained on public reviews struggles with moderate, everyday text it never saw in training.

**4. Non-Response Bias.** Selected people don't participate, and their absence isn't random.

Send a 30-minute burnout survey, and the moderately-stressed employees answer. The genuinely overworked ones — who you most need to hear from — are too underwater to reply.

![fig8 non response](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Laxminarayen/InceptezGenAI-Batch26/main/data/uploads/articles/mrx6uyqk0euyqk-fig8-non-response.jpg)

**_ML impact:_** your morale dashboard glows green right up until key staff start resigning.

**5. Temporal Bias.** Data frozen in one time window gets treated as an ongoing reality.

Train a retail model on March–May 2020 purchases and it "learns" endless toilet paper and zero travel spending. Deploy it today unmodified, and your supply chain orders a warehouse nobody wants.

![fig9.1 temporal](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Laxminarayen/InceptezGenAI-Batch26/main/data/uploads/articles/mrx6xm1bk5snfy-fig9-1-temporal.jpg)

**_ML impact: _**this is concept drift's evil twin — wrong not because the world changed after deployment, but because the training sample was already anomalous.

**6. Feedback-Loop Bias.** The model's own decisions shape the data it trains on next — so the distortion compounds instead of staying still.

A city dispatches pothole repairs based on app reports. High-report neighborhoods get fixed fast, so they keep reporting. Low-report neighborhoods wait, give up, and report even less next cycle.

![fig4 feedback loop](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Laxminarayen/InceptezGenAI-Batch26/main/data/uploads/articles/mrx6ytipovmio4-fig4-feedback-loop.jpg)

The model's own decisions are shaping the data it gets trained on next. That's structurally different from a snapshot bias like undercoverage — it doesn't sit still waiting to be audited, it actively widens the gap on its own. The same pattern shows up in predictive policing (more patrols to over-reported areas generate more arrests there, "confirming" the original bias) and credit scoring (denying credit to a group thins their credit history, "confirming" they're higher risk next cycle).

**Part 4: The Cheat Sheet**

![fig5 cheatsheet](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Laxminarayen/InceptezGenAI-Batch26/main/data/uploads/articles/mrx72q6e7p3jje-fig5-cheatsheet.jpg)

**Rules to Live By**

1.	**Random doesn't mean representative**. Check class balance; use stratified sampling to protect minority classes.
2.	**Audit what's missing, not just what's present**. Ask your team out loud: "Who or what isn't in this dataset, and why?"
3.	**No algorithm fixes bad data**. You can't hyperparameter-tune your way out of survivorship or undercoverage bias — fix it at the source.
4.	**Ask if the bias can feed itsel**f. If your model's outputs shape future training data, a one-time audit isn't enough. Build in a recurring, randomized check that's independent of the model's own past decisions.

author: suru7373
title: Sampling
body:
## **1.What is sampling bias?**

**Sampling Bias:** We select the sample unfairly, flawlessly, tilted.

**Unbiased Sampling:** We select the sample fairly, give a chance to everyone.

Eg: Red & Blue colored marbles in a jar, many red marbles are placed top and also blue marbles are placed under the jar. 
If we close our eyes, pick a sample of marbles as 30 fairly so we get a mixture of 19 red and 11 blue marbles. This is **Unbiased Sampling.**
Suppose we pick a sample of marbles 30 as we open our eyes. We picked the top settled marbles so we got 28 red marbles, 2 blue marbles. This is **Sampling Bias.**

## 2.What are different types of sampling biases?

**Convenience Bias:** One hotel is started up, only we capture the people rating about food on doorstep, instead of entire people of that area.

**Undercoverage Bias:** In the 2026 tamilnadu election assembly, One vote pooling team collected the voting reviews only from the youngsters, because Thalapathy Vijay is attracted by youngsters. They mostly neglect the older generations, senior citizens. Finally we got the successful sampling bias as a result.

**Voluntary Response Bias:** We wouldn’t choose the sample, the people would come to  volunteer as a sample. If we start a new hotel, the QR scanner is placed in the reception for putting a review about food. Most of the time we get the reviews of very very good or very very bad. In this stage, we missed the neutral people like food is okay, not bad.

**Non-Response Bias:** In our college, an interview is conducted, every student gives their number or mail. The company selected a fair, random group of college students to follow up but we wouldn’t give a proper response for it. Because there would not interested that time, sometimes busy at work, internships.,

**Survivorship Bias:** When we are studying a research paper, only we select the successful writers, completely ignoring the failures writer.

**Convenience Bias** (Easiest/Closest) 
**Undercoverage Bias**( Missing Partial group) 
**Voluntary Response** Bias (Self-Selection) 
**Non-Response Bias** (People are selected fairly but refuse to answer or are too busy) 
**Survivorship Bias** (Only looking at the visible "winners" of a process) 

## 3.What are different sampling methods? 
Sampling Methods(Strategies for selecting a sample) 

**A. Probabilistic Sampling Methods (Fair & Random)**

**Simple Random Sampling:** Putting all 3 lakh bank account numbers into a computer algorithm and letting it pick 100 completely at random 

**Stratified Sampling:** The population is divided into sub-groups, like young, middle-aged, old people. Then getting a random sample from those subgroups. 

**Systematic Sampling:** Selecting every k-th person from a list. Like selecting every 10 th person who walks through the college gate. 

**Cluster Sampling:** The population is divided into sub-groups like Stratified Sampling. But we are getting all the people from a few randomly selected groups. 

Difference between Stratified Sampling & Cluster Sampling:
- The first process is the same, the population is divided into subgroups, and the selection process hits different methods.
- In  Stratified Sampling, selecting a random people from every subgroup
- In Cluster Sampling, selecting all people from a random subgroup

**B. Non-Probabilistic Sampling Methods (Judgment-Based)**

**Convenience Sampling:** Surveying people standing next to you because it is easy. 

**Judgment Sampling**: Pick a specific person, because we know they fit the goal. 

**Quota Sampling:** This is the Filling Buckets Method. Imagine you start a new hotel, you want to test your food menu for 100 people, then you decide on a sample from 50 youngsters and 50 seniors.

**Snowball Sampling:** This is a referral-based method. If you want to take a survey about a secret billionaire in Chennai. If you make a random phone call or search street by street. You can’t find those people, because they are so busy, not pick any unknown calls directly. But if you have a billionaire neighbourhood, you ask them to refer any other wealthy people, then your sample size grows like a rolling snowball.

author: asennakesavan
title: Sampling
body:
Sampling Bias:
Sampling bias occurs when the individuals or elements selected for a study are not truly random and do not accurately represent the entire population you are interested in studying. It introduces a systematic error into your research, as certain groups or characteristics are overrepresented or underrepresented in your sample. Simply put, sampling bias is like trying to understand a diverse group of people by only talking to a handful of them.

•	Types of Sampling Bias:
	Self-Selection Bias (Voluntary Response Bias):
Definition: People decide for themselves whether to participate, often those with strong opinions.
Example: An online poll about politics where only highly motivated supporters respond.
	Undercoverage Bias:
Definition: Some groups in the population are systematically left out.
Example: A survey conducted only via smartphones excludes older adults without smartphones.
	Convenience Sampling Bias:
Definition: Sample is chosen from people who are easiest to reach.
Example: Asking only your classmates about city-wide transport issues.
	Survivorship Bias:
Definition: Only successful or surviving cases are studied, ignoring failures.
Example: Studying profitable companies but ignoring those that went bankrupt.
	Exclusion Bias:
Definition: Certain subgroups are deliberately or accidentally excluded.
Example: Studying “students” but leaving out dropouts or home-schooled children.
	Nonresponse Bias:
Definition: When selected participants don’t respond, and their absence skews results.
Example: Sending surveys to households but only hearing back from wealthier families.
	Healthy User Bias:
Definition: In medical studies, healthier or more motivated individuals are more likely to participate.
Example: A fitness app study mostly attracts already active people, not sedentary ones.


Types of Sampling:
•	Probability Sampling (every member has a known chance of selection)
	Random Sampling:
Every member of the population has an equal chance of being selected.
Example: Picking names from a hat.
	Systematic Sampling:
Select every kth member from a list after a random start.
Example: Choosing every 10th person in a queue.
	Stratified Sampling:
Divide the population into subgroups (strata) like age or gender, then sample proportionally from each.
Example: Ensuring equal representation of men and women in a survey.
	Cluster Sampling:
Divide the population into clusters (groups), then randomly select entire clusters.
Example: Choosing a few schools at random and surveying all students in those schools.
•	Non-Probability Sampling (not everyone has a chance)
	Convenience Sampling:
Select people who are easiest to reach.
Example: Asking friends or nearby shoppers.
	Quota Sampling:
Ensure the sample meets certain quotas (e.g., 50% male, 50% female).
Example: Interviewing until you reach the required numbers.
	Snowball Sampling:
Existing participants recruit new participants.
Example: Studying rare communities where members refer you to others.
	Purposive (Judgmental) Sampling:
Researcher deliberately selects individuals who fit specific criteria.
Example: Choosing only doctors for a study on medical practices.
